in_context.text: This is the opening line of a letter. Paul names himself and states his authority as an apostle sent by God's command, before greeting Timothy in the next verse. It sets up a letter whose first task is to confront false teachers in Ephesus.

speaker.text: Paul the apostle, who names himself here. Traditionally he is the author. Many critical scholars think a follower wrote in his name, while others defend Paul's authorship.

audience.text: Timothy, Paul's younger co-worker and "own son in the faith," whom Paul had left to lead the church at Ephesus.

affected.text: The church in Ephesus, especially the people teaching "other doctrine." Paul's stated authority backs Timothy as he corrects them.

what.text: Paul claims his apostleship came "by the commandment of God our Saviour, and Lord Jesus Christ." He did not appoint himself. He also calls Christ "our hope."

events.text: Paul had urged Timothy to stay in Ephesus while Paul went on into Macedonia.

written.text: Traditional view: about AD 62-64, between Paul's two Roman imprisonments. Scholarly view: many critical scholars date it around AD 80-110. Others defend the earlier date.

where.text: The letter went to Ephesus, a wealthy port and capital of the Roman province of Asia. Where it was written is not stated, but Paul may have been in Macedonia.

purpose.text: By grounding his role in God's command, Paul gives weight to the instructions that follow. Those instructions tell Timothy to stop false teaching and lead the church.

big_picture.text: Paul often opens letters by stating that his apostleship comes from God, not from people. Titus 1:3 uses the same phrase, "according to the commandment of God our Saviour."

for_readers.text: The verse presents God as Saviour and Christ as the believer's hope. Colossians 1:27 echoes this when it calls Christ "the hope of glory."

why_it_matters.text: The word means a messenger or "one sent on a mission." In the New Testament it marks an apostle of Christ. Paul claims equality with the Twelve, so this is a claim of authority, not just a job title.
Epitagē means a command, a word also used of divine commands. Paul presents his mission as an order from God, not his own choice.
Sōtēr means deliverer or preserver. In Paul's day it was a common title for kings. Here it is given to God, as in the Old Testament.
In the New Testament, elpis is always an expectation of good. Calling Christ "our hope" means confident expectation, not wishful thinking.

takeaway.text: This verse is a greeting that sets out Paul's credentials. He speaks as one sent by God's command, with Christ as the hope behind his message.

unsupported.reason: The lexicon says only that NT elpis is always an expectation of good. It does not say the hope is confident or certain, and 1 Peter 1:3's 'lively hope' does not establish 'confident expectation, not wishful thinking.'
